text: Installing Terraform and declaring a provider only gets you ready to run it. The actual workflow is three commands, always in this order: init, plan, apply. This lesson walks through each one in depth, including exactly what real plan output looks like and what those create, destroy, and update symbols mean.

terraform init prepares the working directory. Against last lesson's required_providers block, it downloads the azurerm provider into a hidden .terraform folder, sets up the backend that stores state — a local terraform.tfstate file, by default — and writes .terraform.lock.hcl, pinning the exact provider version resolved so a teammate running init later gets the same one. Run it again whenever a provider or module changes; running it with nothing changed is harmless.

terraform plan is a dry run, full stop — it does not touch your cloud subscription. It reads your configuration and current state, refreshes its knowledge of each resource's real values from the provider's API, and diffs declared config against state. Against an empty state with one resource group declared, you'd see a plus sign next to a new azurerm_resource_group, its attributes listed, and a summary line — Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.

Those symbols are the entire vocabulary you need to read any plan. Plus means it will be created. Minus means it will be destroyed. Tilde means it will be updated in place — changed without destroying and recreating it. Change a resource group's location after it's already applied, and plan again shows a tilde next to that attribute instead of a plus, because that's an update, not a brand-new resource. Some changes do force a destroy-and-recreate instead, and plan always tells you which one you're looking at.

terraform apply runs that same plan and shows it to you the same way — but then, only if you type yes at the confirmation prompt, it actually executes it. That prompt is a real safety feature: anything other than yes cancels with nothing changed. Once confirmed, Terraform calls the real Azure API through the azurerm provider, creates the resource group, and reports back — Apply complete, one added, zero changed, zero destroyed.

The moment apply finishes, Terraform writes that result into terraform.tfstate. That file is exactly what the next lesson is about — how Terraform uses its own record of what it's managing, rather than the live cloud, to decide what plan and apply do the next time you run them, and why that distinction matters more than it sounds like it should.
